stories.title: Tigray's fragile recovery at risk as drone strikes reignite war fears
stories.summary: Over the past month, drone strikes have hit several parts of Ethiopia's Tigray region, sparking fears of a renewed war. The last conflict left an estimated 600,000 people dead, making it the deadliest conflict of the 21st century. As the region has not yet rebuilt or recovered from that damage, health experts are warning of the potential impact on patients if another war were to break out. FRANCE 24's Tom Canetty reports.

stories.title: #Nepal: Two flood survivors rescued from hydropower tunnel
stories.summary: In a video posted to social media on September 4, the Nepali #army announced it had rescued two workers trapped in a hydropower tunnel. The rescue brings hope of reaching over a dozen others thought to be trapped inside the tunnel. Both men were flown to a hospital in #Kathmandu. The floods killed more than 1,200 people, and over 5,000 are still missing.

stories.title: IOM ramps up emergency aid in Lake Chad as thousands flee Boko Haram
stories.summary: More than 75,000 people have been newly displaced within Chad’s Lake Province following a resurgence in Boko Haram attacks in recent months. That is the latest figure from the International Organization for Migration, which is providing emergency assistance to meet their most immediate needs. Most of these tens of thousands of people have fled the islands of Lake Chad, seeking safety in towns and villages further away from the island areas. FRANCE 24's Harold Girard reports.

stories.title: From forced labour to World Heritage: Sao Tome's colonial plantations
stories.summary: Sao Tome and Principe's "Rocas" – colonial-era plantations – have been added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2026, in recognition of their architecture and their fundamental importance to the country’s history. While the majority of them now lie derelict, they are attracting increasing interest from investors keen to develop the tourism potential of the history-steeped buildings.

stories.title: Thailand freezes 49 data centres as resource fears escalate
stories.summary: With data centres draining power and water, the government is now rethinking its approach.
article_sentences: Thailand has suspended construction of 49 data centres to develop new regulations addressing environmental and resource concerns.
The government aims to create uniform standards to ensure sustainable growth of the data centre industry.
Rapid tech investment has raised issues of power and water use, prompting higher scrutiny and possible increased electricity rates for large operators.

Thailand’s embrace of data centres hit a speed bump after the government suspended construction of 49 server farms as public concerns about the power-hungry facilities’ impact on communities intensified.

The projects were halted to give officials time to develop new industry regulations, expected to be announced in a month, Danucha Pichayanan, secretary-general of the National Economic and Social Development Council, said at a news briefing on Sept 4.
Danucha spoke after the first meeting of Thailand’s data centres supervision commission, led by Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas.
“Today’s decision doesn’t mean Thailand is closing the door to data-centres investment because the industry is critical to the country’s competitiveness,” Ekniti said.
“We simply want clear and consistent standards in place to ensure the industry can grow sustainably.”
Thailand will establish uniform oversight of data centres in operation, as well as those being developed, Danucha said.
Governments the world over are tightening oversight of data centres as the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence has led to a surge in such facilities.

Global data centres spending is set to reach US$31.6 trillion (S$40 trillion) through 2050 to meet the world’s growing appetite for AI, an investment boom with no precedent in history, according to PricewaterhouseCoopers.
At the same time, the tech industry, led by US giants such as Microsoft and Amazon.com, is trying to blunt a backlash against data centres that threatens to slow the buildout.

stories.title: Italy weighs the results as Giorgia Meloni’s government sets a longevity record
stories.summary: In a country where governments are famously short-lived, the perceived success of Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has often been attributed to her survival skills rather than her accomplishments. The record is likely to boost the prime minister's image as Italy, which has had almost 70 governments over the past 80 years, gears up for a national vote in 2027, analysts say. But recent events have complicated her path to re-election.

stories.title: Putin to hold talks with Vietnamese president on September 9
stories.summary: The leaders are to discuss the state and prospects for the further development of the Russia-Vietnam comprehensive strategic partnership
article_sentences: Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold talks at the Kremlin on September 9 with General Secretary of the Central Committee of Vietnam's Communist Party and the country's President To Lam, who will be paying a state visit to Russia, the presidential press service reported.
"The leaders will discuss the state and prospects for the further development of the Russia-Vietnam comprehensive strategic partnership.
The talks’ key topics will include trade, economic, scientific and educational ties, humanitarian exchanges, and cooperation in security and defense.
They will also discuss current international and regional issues," the statement said.
A package of bilateral documents is expected to be adopted following the meeting.

stories.title: Nigerian police arrest four suspects over alleged organ harvesting
stories.summary: In Nigeria, the police have arrested four suspects over alleged organ harvesting. Two of the suspects are medical doctors who are accused of carrying out the surgeries to harvest the kidneys. The victims are mainly vulnerable and uneducated youths whose financial desperation is exploited to illegally harvest their kidney for transplant to patients who are often wealthy, as FRANCE 24’s Sam Olukoya reports.
